tip: 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo) works morning, noon, and night — Korean's one all-day hello.
안녕히 가세요 (annyeonghi gaseyo) to the person leaving; 안녕히 계세요 (gyeseyo) to the one staying.
도 replaces 은/는 to say 'too': 저도 (jeodo = me too).
이에요 after a consonant, 예요 after a vowel: 수진이에요 (Sujin-ieyo), 민수예요 (Minsu-yeyo).
Korean drops 'your' — 이름이 뭐예요? (ireumi mwoyeyo) is literally 'name is what?'
제 (je) = my, the humble form of 저의: 제 이름 (je ireum = my name).
No word for 'you' needed — use the name + 씨: 민수 씨예요? (Minsu ssi-yeyo = are you Minsu?)
제가 (jega) is 'I', not 'my' – 저 (jeo) plus subject marker 가 (ga), fused. It spotlights you as the answer: 네, 제가 민수예요 (ne, jega Minsu-yeyo = yes, I'm the one who's Minsu).
To introduce someone politely, Korean points at 'this side': 이쪽은 제 친구예요 (ijjogeun je chinguyeyo = this side is my friend) – softer than pointing at the person.
-세요 respects the person you talk about: 선생님이세요 (seonsaengnim-iseyo = is [my] teacher).
어느 나라 사람이에요? (eoneu nara saramieyo) — literally 'which country person?' — asks nationality.
은/는 marks the topic — 은 after consonants, 는 after vowels: 저는 (jeoneun), 씨는 (ssi-neun).
Yes/no questions keep the same words — just a rising tone: 사람이에요? (saramieyo?)
'Is not X' = X이/가 아니에요: 중국 사람이 아니에요 (sarami anieyo = am not Chinese).
교사 (gyosa) is the neutral job title for your own work: 저는 교사예요 (jeoneun gyosayeyo). 선생님 (seonsaengnim) honors others – never use it for yourself.
감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) is formal-polite — the safe thank-you for staff, elders, strangers.
죄송해요 (joesonghaeyo) is the everyday polite 'sorry' — bump into someone, say it.
괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) covers 'it's fine,' 'no problem,' and 'I'm OK' — one word, many uses.
아니에요 (anieyo) after thanks = 'not at all / you're welcome.'
저기요 (jeogiyo) is literally 'over there' – it's how you hail a waiter or a stranger without knowing their name.
고마워요 (gomawoyo) is warm, everyday thanks for people you know; 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) is the formal step up for strangers and staff.
Korean drops pronouns when clear — 학생이에요 (haksaengieyo) alone means 'I'm a student.'
이 = near me, 그 = near you, 저 = far from both: 이거/그거/저거 (igeo/geugeo/jeogeo).

english: That over there is our house.
tip: Koreans say 우리 (uri = our) even for their own home or family: 우리 집 (uri jip = my house).
(으)로 = 'in / by means of': 한국어로 (hangugeo-ro) = in Korean.
Korean 'have' is 'exist': 있어요 (isseoyo) = there is / I have; 없어요 (eopseoyo) = don't have.
을/를 marks the object — 을 after a consonant, 를 after a vowel: 물을 마셔요 (mur-eul masyeoyo = I drink water).
사요 means 'buy' — one letter from 싸요 (ssayo = cheap): 사과를 사요 (sagwa-reul sayo = I buy apples).
좋아해요 (joahaeyo = like) takes 을/를 (eul/reul): 김치를 좋아해요 (gimchi-reul joahaeyo). Its twin 좋아요 (joayo = is good) flips to 이/가 (i/ga): 김치가 좋아요 (gimchi-ga joayo).
들어요 covers both 'listen' and 'hear': 음악을 들어요 (eumag-eul deureoyo = I listen to music).
